How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Facial expressions are central to human social interaction, yet reliably quantifying how faces move over time remains challenging. Here, we address these limitations in three ways. First, we leverage photorealistic MetaHuman animations with precisely specified facial motion to systematically evaluate two widely used AU detection systems: AFAR and OpenFace. Four avatars were animated with identical motion parameters to generate 72 videos comprising single-AU and AU-combination sequences. Although both systems performed above chance, their performance varied substantially across AUs and avatars. Second, we introduce and validate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry, yielding consistent and robust motion estimates across avatars and animations. Third, we provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework.

Together, our findings reveal systematic biases in current AU-detection systems, highlight the potential of landmark-based analysis to characterize facial motion directly, and provide an open, reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion and evaluating the methods used to capture it.

Introduction

Facial expressions are vital for human communication and social interaction, allowing observers to infer others' emotions, intentions and mental states. Although faces are inherently dynamic, much of face perception research has relied on static images (Dawel et al., 2021).

Yet, psychophysical and neuroimaging evidence consistently shows that facial motion provides important information for face perception (Krumhuber et al., 2023). The human visual system is highly sensitive to the precise dynamics of facial motion (Dobs et al., 2014), and dynamic compared with static stimuli can enhance face and expression recognition, particularly when expressions are subtle or ambiguous (Richoz et al., 2024; Yovel & O'Toole, 2016).

Neuroimaging studies further suggest partly distinct neural mechanisms for processing dynamic and static faces (Bernstein & Yovel, 2015; Duchaine & Yovel, 2015; Pitcher et al., 2014; Pitcher & Ungerleider, 2021; Prabhakar et al., 2026; Puce, 2024). Together, these findings highlight the importance of facial motion for understanding face perception. However, studying facial motion requires methods that allow researchers not only to generate naturalistic yet experimentally controlled dynamic face stimuli, but also to reliably quantify how faces move over time.

A variety of approaches have been used to create dynamic face stimuli, each involving different trade-offs between naturalism and experimental control (Dobs et al., 2018). Real face videos offer high ecological validity but provide limited control over facial motion parameters (Dawel et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). Conversely, 3D computer-generated (CG) faces afford fine-grained parametrization (Egger et al., 2020; Grewe et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025), but may appear less natural or evoke uncanny responses (Crookes et al., 2015; Di Natale et al., 2023; Vaitonytė et al., 2023), and can produce altered behavioral and neural responses compared with real faces (Kätsyri et al., 2020; Kegel et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2023). Importantly, these limitations diminish with increasing photorealism: both perceived eeriness and neural differences relative to real faces are reduced for highly realistic CG stimuli (Higgins et al., 2021; Nasser Oesterreich et al., 2025; Schindler et al., 2017). Recent advances in graphics technology may therefore help overcome the traditional trade-off between naturalism and experimental control when generating dynamic face stimuli.

One such platform is Unreal Engine's MetaHuman (MH) framework (Epic Games, 2019), which provides freely accessible photorealistic avatars with detailed facial rigs that enable precise control over anatomically plausible facial motion (Giuliana, 2022). MH avatars have recently been adopted across media, education, and experimental psychology (Bae et al., 2025; Haddick et al., 2022). Comparative work shows that MH stimuli appear more humanlike than other digital human systems (Bae et al., 2025) and can reduce the uncanny valley effects commonly associated with CG faces (Fraser et al., 2024; Haddick et al., 2022; Mori et al., 2012). Recent datasets further demonstrate that MH avatars are perceived as realistic, friendly, and likable across diverse samples (Tsenkova et al., 2025). Critically, their rig-based parametrization allows facial motion to be precisely specified across time and reproduced across different identities. This combination of photorealism and experimental control makes MH avatars particularly well suited for generating dynamic facial stimuli with known underlying motion.

To quantify facial motion in dynamic stimuli, researchers commonly rely on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) (Ekman et al., 2002), an anatomically grounded framework that decomposes facial expressions into individual Action Units (AUs) defined by the underlying musculature (Zhi et al., 2020). For example, a smile involves contraction of the zygomatic major muscle, which pulls up the lip corners (AU12), often accompanied by activation of the outer portion of the orbicularis oculi, which raises the cheeks (AU6). Manual FACS coding, however, is highly labor-intensive, requiring extensive training and frame-wise annotation of video sequences (Girard & Cohn, 2016; Stöckli et al., 2018). As a result, automated AU detection systems such as OpenFace (Baltrusaitis et al., 2016) and the AFAR toolbox (Ertugrul et al., 2019a) are increasingly used to quantify facial behavior. Despite their widespread adoption in psychological and behavioral research (Ambrosen et al., 2025; Darzi et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2018; Hickman et al., 2022; Hirsch et al., 2023; Namba et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), the performance and potential biases of these systems remain insufficiently understood (Ertugrul et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2023; Namba et al., 2021). Characterizing such biases is particularly difficult using naturalistic video datasets, in which the underlying facial motion is not precisely known. Controlled dynamic stimuli with known motion parameters therefore provide an important opportunity to systematically evaluate automated AU detection and determine how reliably these systems capture the specified facial motion.

Complementary to AU-based approaches, facial motion can be quantified more directly from changes in facial geometry. Landmark-based approaches track the positions of anatomically defined facial points across time and characterize motion through changes in their positions, distances, or spatial configurations (Ko, 2018; Rajan et al., 2019). Such approaches have been used, for example, to distinguish spontaneous from posed smiles and more broadly to characterize facial expressions for automatic emotion recognition (Park et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2018). Unlike AU detection, these approaches do not require observed facial motion to be classified into predefined action categories, providing a complementary description of where and how much the face moves. However, the extent to which landmark-based measures reliably capture known facial motion across different identities and types of facial movement remains unclear.

Here, we use controlled facial animations in which motion parameters are precisely specified and reproduced across photorealistic MH avatars to achieve three aims. First, we systematically evaluate the performance and potential biases of widely used automated AU detection systems. Second, we develop and evaluate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies facial motion from tracked geometry. Third, we introduce the open-source Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET), which integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework for applying and systematically benchmarking facial motion quantification methods.

Materials and Methods

Action Unit Animations

To systematically evaluate methods for quantifying facial motion, we created controlled facial animations with precisely specified motion parameters using the MetaHuman (MH) plugin (MetaHuman Creator, 2022) in Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) (Unreal Engine 5, 2022), an advanced 3D graphics engine. Four freely available MH avatars were selected from the plugin's library (two male, two female; estimated ages 20-50 years; Figure 1A). Animations were generated in Python 3.10.6 using the UE5 Python API, which provides programmatic access to the facial rig system. The UE5 facial rig is based on FACS (Ekman et al., 2002), allowing frame-by-frame manipulation of individual AUs through continuous activation parameters ranging from 0 to 1. This enabled precise control over AU onset, peak, and offset timing. These resulting frame-wise AU activation trajectories served as the ground truth for subsequent evaluation of the facial motion quantification methods. Critically, identical motion parameters were applied to all four avatars, allowing us to assess the consistency of facial motion estimates across different faces while holding the underlying animation parameters constant.

For each avatar, we created 18 animations, yielding 72 animations in total. Animations were of two types: single-AU animations (n=11) and AU-combination animations (n=7) (Table 1). Single-AU animations allowed us to evaluate individual facial movements in isolation, whereas AU-combination animations provided more complex patterns of co-occurring facial motion. Each animation comprised 60 frames and began with a neutral face. In single-AU animations, the target AU increased linearly from 0 to its peak activation (i.e., 1) at the midpoint of the sequence and returned to neutral by the final frame (Figure 1B). The single AUs were restricted to those available as outputs in both AU detection systems: AU1, AU2, AU4, AU6, AU7, AU10, AU12, AU14, AU15, AU17, AU23 (Table 1).

AU-combination animations combined the eyebrow-related AUs (AU1, AU2, AU4)

with one lower-face AU (e.g., AU10, AU12 or AU14; Table 1). To approximate the temporal unfolding of more complex facial movements, AU1, AU2, and AU4 peaked sequentially at frames 15, 30, and 45, respectively, with each returning to neutral 15 frames after its peak (Figure 1B). Lower-face AUs increased from neutral, peaked at frame 30, and maintained nonzero activation throughout the animation except for the first and final frames.

All animations were rendered as 30-fps videos in AVI format at a resolution of 720 x 1280 pixels. Overview of the Animation and Analysis Pipeline QUANTIFYING FACIAL MOTION WITH REALISTIC AVATARS 8 Notes. (A) Four photorealistic MetaHuman avatars were animated frame-by-frame in Unreal Engine 5 to generate 18 controlled facial motion sequences per avatar (11 single-AU and 7 AU-combination sequences), yielding 72 animations in total. For each sequence, AU intensities were precisely specified across 60 frames. (B) Ground-truth AU intensity matrices for an example single-AU animation (AU12; left) and an AU-combination animation (BrowsAU10; right). (C) Schematic overview of the automated AU detection tools (OpenFace and AFAR) used to estimate AU intensities from the rendered videos. (D) Predicted AU intensity matrices for the same example animations. Both systems capture aspects of the ground-truth motion but also show false alarms and misses.

Facial Motion Quantification

The facial motion quantification and analysis procedures described below are implemented in the Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET), which is described in detail after the individual methods. Corresponding FACET functions are provided 195 throughout the Methods where applicable. 196

Automated Action Unit Detection Systems 197

We evaluated two open-source AU detection systems: OpenFace (OF, v.2.2.0; 198 Baltrusaitis et al., 2016) and the Automated Facial Affect Recognition toolbox (AFAR, v.1.0.0; 199 Ertugrul et al., 2019a). These tools were selected because they are widely used for automated 200 facial behavior analysis in vision science, affective computing, and psychological research. 201

Both systems have been validated on established facial expression datasets and provide frame-202 wise AU predictions suitable for analyzing dynamic stimuli. All animation videos were 203 processed using the OF executable (v2.2.0, 64-bit) on Windows 11, while a custom MATLAB 204 script (version R2020a) was used to batch-process the videos with AFAR. Both systems follow 205 a broadly similar processing pipeline involving face detection and alignment, estimation of 206 head pose and facial landmarks, face registration, and AU prediction (Figure 1C). OF provides two types of AU outputs: (1) binary AU occurrence (0 = absent,1 = present) and ( 2) continuous AU intensity estimates ranging from 0 to 5 (0 = none,5 = maximum intensity). AFAR provides continuous AU probability estimates ranging from 0 to 1. To place the continuous outputs of both systems on a common numerical scale, we used OF intensity estimates rather than binary occurrence estimates and linearly rescaled them to the 0-1 range (facet.au_detection.metrics.normalize_detector_outputs). All 72 animations were processed with both OF and AFAR, yielding frame-wise AU predictions for each sequence (Figure 1D).

Subsequent analyses were restricted to AUs available as outputs in both systems (Table 1).

For classification analyses, continuous outputs were converted to binary AU-presence estimates using a common threshold of 0.2 (facet.au_detection.config). FACS distinguishes five levels of AU intensity, ranging from A (trace or barely visible) to E (maximum intensity) (Ekman & Friesen, 2019; Ekman et al., 2002). Previous evaluations of automated AU detection systems on datasets not used for model training have used level A as the criterion for AU presence (Ertugrul et al., 2020; Zhi et al., 2020). Accordingly, we used 0.2 as a common operational threshold for classification analyses across systems. On the rescaled OF intensity scale, this corresponds to the lowest FACS intensity level; for AFAR, it represents a probability threshold applied for comparability.

We additionally evaluated two more recent AU detection systems, PyAFAR (v4.0.0; Hinduja et al., 2023) and PyFeat (v1.0.0; Cheong et al., 2023). PyAFAR was not included in the primary comparison because continuous AU intensity estimates were available for only five of the AUs included in our stimulus set (AU6, AU10, AU12, AU14 and AU17), preventing a comparable evaluation across the full set of AUs. PyFeat was evaluated using the same classification procedure and showed substantially higher false-positive rates than OF and AFAR (average TPR and FPR score > 0.5), making its predictions difficult to interpret. We therefore focus the main analyses on OF and AFAR but report the PyFeat results in the Supplementary Materials (Suppl. Fig. 1).

Landmark Displacement Analysis

As a complementary approach to AU-based motion quantification, we developed a pipeline that directly characterizes facial motion from landmark displacements (Figure 4A).

We used OF's facial landmark extraction module, which provides 3D coordinates for 51 within-face landmarks alongside the AU predictions. Although the present animations were rendered from a fixed frontal viewpoint with minimal rigid motion, we implemented a rigidmotion correction procedure to facilitate application of the pipeline to videos containing head movement. Using OF's frame-wise estimates of 3D translation (x,y,z) and head rotation (roll, pitch, yaw), translation vectors were first subtracted from the raw landmark coordinates, after which the inverse rotation matrix for each frame was applied to remove rigid head-motion components (facet.au_detection.landmarks.inverse_affine_transform). The resulting coordinates were then mean-centered across landmarks to remove residual global positional offsets.

Facial motion was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the corrected 3D position of each landmark at each frame and its position in the initial neutral frame, yielding a 51 x 60 landmark-displacement matrix for each animation. Because displacement was calculated relative to each avatar's own neutral configuration, static differences in facial geometry across avatars did not directly contribute to the displacement measure. Displacement values therefore represent the magnitude of nonrigid landmark movement in 3D space relative to the neutral configuration.

We characterized the resulting displacement profiles using two complementary analyses. First, to assess the consistency of facial motion across avatars, we computed pairwise correlations (Pearson's r) between the displacement matrices of different avatars for each animation (facet.au_detection.displacement_analysis.compute_pairwise_displacement_ correlations). We summarized these correlations both across animations for each avatar pair, to assess overall consistency across faces, and across avatar pairs for each animation, to determine whether cross-avatar consistency varied across facial movements. Then, to evaluate whether displacement was spatially concentrated in facial regions expected to move for a given AU, we calculated the ratio between the mean displacement of AU-relevant landmarks and the mean displacement of all remaining landmarks (facet.au_detection.displacement_analysis.compute_expected_motion_ratio). For example, for an AU1 animation, the expected-to-be-active set comprised eyebrow landmarks. A ratio

Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET)

Methods for quantifying facial motion are implemented across different software environments, rely on distinct dependencies, and vary in their input requirements, processing interfaces, and output structures. These differences can make it cumbersome to process larger datasets, combine multiple methods within a single analysis pipeline, and compare their outputs in a standardized manner. To address these challenges, we developed the Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET), an open-source Python toolbox that provides a unified framework for applying and systematically benchmarking facial motion quantification methods.

FACET integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a consistent application programming interface (API). It provides standardized input handling and batch processing of multiple files, allowing users to run supported AU detectors, quantify facial motion from landmark displacement, and generate corresponding visualizations within a common workflow. FACET can additionally convert detector-specific outputs into a standardized BIDS-like format, allowing downstream analyses to operate on a common data structure irrespective of the original detector or output format (e.g., .mat or .npy). FACET can be installed as a Python package or run within a Docker container, facilitating reproducible use across computing environments.

The analyses reported in the present study were originally conducted using the individual software environments described above, reflecting heterogeneous workflows currently required to combine different facial analysis tools. FACET integrates these analysis steps within a common framework, and we provide the corresponding FACET functions alongside each analysis below. This allows researchers to reproduce the present analyses, apply individual components to their own data, and use controlled stimuli with known motion parameters to benchmark facial motion quantification methods.

Statistical Analyses

Classification Metrics

We evaluated frame-wise classification performance for each AU across all animations.

Ground-truth AU activation values were extracted directly from the animation parameters for each frame. Frames with ground-truth AU activation > 0.2 were considered AU-present, and the rest were considered AU-absent. To obtain binary predictions for the calculation of trueand false-positive rates, continuous AU outputs from both detection systems were converted to binary occurrence values (0 = absent,1 = present) using the common threshold of 0.2 defined above.

To assess each system's ability to discriminate between the presence and absence of an

Temporal Alignment Analysis

To examine how well each AU detection system captured the temporal dynamics of AU activation, we quantified the correspondence between predicted AU time series and the ground-truth activation trajectories specified by the facial rig in UE5. For each AU and animation, predicted and ground-truth time series were z-normalized, and their crosscorrelation was calculated at zero lag. At zero lag, the normalized cross-correlation is equivalent to the Pearson correlation coefficient (r), with higher values indicating greater similarity in the temporal profile of predicted and ground-truth AU activation across frames.

This measure therefore captures temporal alignment in the shape of the activation trajectories rather than agreement in their absolute magnitude. FACET additionally supports lagged crosscorrelation and further analyses of temporal dynamics through its au_detection.temporal module.

Results

Binary Classification Performance

To assess how well automated AU detection captured the specified facial motion in our controlled animations, we first evaluated classification performance using ROC AUC (Figure 2A). Across systems, performance was significantly above chance (M = 0.69, SD = 0.20; t(143) = 11.3, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.94). Overall AUC did not differ significantly between OF (M = 0.71, SD = 0.19) and AFAR (M = 0.67, SD = 0.21; t(71) = 1.39, p = .17, Cohen's d = 0.19).

Across both systems, overall AUC did not differ significantly across avatars (F(1, 3) = 0.98, p = .508, η² = 0.49), whereas performance varied across animations (F(1, 17) = 2.303, p = .047, η² = 0.7). Evaluating individual AU performance across single-AU and AUcombination animations (Figure 2A) showed that both systems performed well (AUC > .80) for single-AU animations AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.92, SD = 0.03) and AU7 (lid tightener; M = 0.91, SD = 0.15). OF additionally performed well on AU10 (upper lip raiser; M = 0.93, SD = 0.01) and AU12 (lip corner puller; M = 0.82, SD = 0.03), whereas AFAR showed high AUC for AU23 (lip tightener; M = 0.96, SD = 0.08) and AU15 (lip corner depressor; M = 0.84, SD = 0.13). In contrast, AU6 (cheek raiser) yielded below-chance AUC (< 0.50) across both systems (M = 0.27, SD = 0.07). Low AUC was also observed for AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 0.48, SD = 0.07) in OF and AU-combination animation browsAU12 in AFAR (eyebrow motions and lip corner puller; M = 0.44, SD = 0.04). Thus, although average classification performance was above chance, it varied substantially across facial expressions.

To further characterize detection performance, we evaluated true-positive (TPR) and false-positive (FPR) rates. As for AUC, TPR did not significantly differ between AFAR (M = 0.33, SD = 0.30) and OF (M = 0.30, SD = 0.29; W = 752.0, p = .43, rRBC = -0.12). AFAR, however, showed a significantly higher FPR (M = 0.13, SD = 0.12) than OF (M = 0.06, SD = 0.07; W = 304.5, p < .001, rRBC = -0.76). Because our subsequent analyses focused on whether detection performance varied systematically across avatars and facial animations rather than on differences between the two detection systems, TPR and FPR were averaged across systems for these analyses.

Comparisons Across Avatars

Both TPR and FPR differed significantly across avatars (TPR: χ 2 (3) = 20.434, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.38; FPR: χ 2 (3) = 43.022, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.80). Post-hoc comparisons showed that both metrics were consistently higher for the two male avatars (Cooper and Garry) than for the two female avatars (Ada and Pia; Figure 2B). Importantly, the simultaneous increase in TPR and FPR suggests an increased tendency to predict AU presence for male avatars, rather than uniformly better detection performance. However, given the small number of avatars (two male, two female), these differences cannot be attributed specifically to avatar sex and may reflect other differences in facial form or appearance.

Comparisons Across Animations

Both TPR and FPR varied substantially across animations (TPR: χ²(17) = 44.8, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.66; FPR: χ²(17) = 51.51, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.76; Figure 2C).

Animations of AU7 (lid tightener), AU12 (lip corner puller) and AU14 (dimpler) yielded the highest TPRs, whereas AU6 (cheek raiser), AU2 (outer brow raiser) and AU17 (chin raiser) yielded the lowest.

FPRs also varied systematically across facial movements. Several animations involving smiling-related movements, particularly browsAU12, AU12, and browsAU10, produced high FPRs, whereas AU4 (brow lowerer), AU23 (lip tightener) and browsAll showed comparatively low FPRs. The combination of high TPR and elevated FPR for smile-related movements (especially AU12, lip corner puller) suggests an increased tendency of the systems to predict smile-related AUs.

Overall, OF and AFAR showed moderate classification performance, with substantial variation across facial movements and avatars. Although average AUC did not differ across avatars, threshold-based analyses revealed systematic avatar-dependent differences in both true-and false-positive rates. Classification performance also varied strongly across AUs, with high performance for some facial movements but poor discrimination or elevated false-positive rates for others. Together, these findings show that automated AU detection does not capture different facial movements and faces equally reliably, even when the underlying AU activation trajectories are precisely controlled.

Temporal Alignment

To evaluate how well each system captured the temporal dynamics of the specified facial motion, we quantified the correspondence between predicted AU and ground-truth activation trajectories (Figure 1B, D). Overall, temporal alignment was relatively low (Figure 3A). OF predictions showed significantly higher correlations with the ground truth (M = 0.36, QUANTIFYING FACIAL MOTION WITH REALISTIC AVATARS 20 SD = 0.29, Median = 0.41) than AFAR predictions (M = 0.26, SD = 0.32, Median = 0.22 ; W = 895, p = .019, rRBC = 0.32).

Averaged across systems, temporal alignment did not differ significantly across avatars (χ 2 (3) = 3.533, p = .316, Kendall's W = 0.07), but varied substantially across animations (χ 2 (17) = 36.193, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.53). For 15 of 18 animations, mean correlations were below 0.50. The highest correspondence was observed for AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.56, SD = 0.16), AU7 (lid tightener; M = 0.55, SD = 0.42), and AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 0.51, SD = 0.38). In contrast, AU6 (cheek raiser; M = -0.12, SD = 0.03) and AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 0.04, SD = 0.19) showed particularly low alignment. For several AUs, temporal alignment was higher for the AU-combination animations than in the corresponding single-AU animations, including AU23 (browsAU23; M = 0.40, SD = 0.13), AU15 (browsAU15; M = 0.37, SD = 0.20), and AU10 (browsAU10; M = 0.37, SD = 0.20).

We next examined these patterns separately for the two detection systems (Figure 3B-C). For OF, temporal alignment differed significantly across avatars (χ²(3) = 12, p = .007, Kendall's W = 0.22), with the highest correspondence for Ada (M = 0.48, SD = 0.31) being significantly higher than the lowest correspondence for Cooper (M = 0.3, SD = 0.27; p = 0.003).

No significant avatar effect was observed for AFAR (χ²(3) = 0.2, p = .98, Kendall's W = 0.004).

Temporal alignment varied significantly across animations for both OF (χ²(17) = 49.84, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.73) and AFAR (χ²(17) = 31.84, p = .015, Kendall's W = 0.47).

For OF, correspondence was lowest for AU6 (cheek raiser; M = -0.12, SD = 0.02), AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = -0.01, SD = 0.07), and AU23 (lip tightener; M = 0, SD = 0.15), and highest for AU7 (lid tightener; M = 0.88, SD = 0.05), animations involving AU10 (upper lip raiser; M = 0.62, SD = 0.12; browsAU10: M = 0.53, SD = 0.04), and AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.61, SD = 0.19; browsAU14: M = 0.5, SD = 0.1). For AFAR, correspondence was lowest for AU6 (M = -0.13, SD = 0.03), AU17 (chin raiser; M = -0.02, SD = 0.13) and browsAU12 (AU-combination involving lip corner puller; M = 0.03, SD = 0.03), and highest for AU23 (lip tightener; M = 0.7, SD = 0.39), AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 0.54, SD = 0.51) and AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.50, SD = 0.12).

Together, these results show that above-chance classification of AU presence does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of its temporal dynamics. Temporal alignment with the specified AU trajectories was generally low and varied substantially across facial movements and detection systems. Landmark Displacement Analysis

To quantify facial motion independently of the AU prediction step, we computed displacement across 51 within-face landmarks for all 72 animations (Figure 4A). Landmark positions were obtained using OF's facial landmark tracker, but the subsequent analyses did not rely on its AU predictions.

Consistency Across Avatars

Because identical facial rigging parameters were applied across avatars, a consistent motion descriptor should yield similar displacement patterns across avatars for the same animation. Overall, cross-avatar consistency was high, with a mean pairwise correlation of r = 0.87 (SD = 0.13) across animations. Moreover, mean correlations exceeded .80 for every avatar pair (Figure 4B), indicating that landmark displacement yielded highly consistent estimates of facial motion across the four avatars.

Next, we examined whether cross-avatar consistency varied across facial movements (Figure 4C). With the exception of AU7 (lid tightener), all animations showed mean crossavatar correlations above 0.70. The highest consistency was observed for AU12 (lip corner puller; M = 0.98, SD = 0.01), browsAU10 (M = 0.98, SD = 0.01), AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 0.97, SD = 0.02), AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 0.96, SD = 0.01), AU10 (upper lip raiser; M = 0.95, SD = 0.01), and AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.95, SD = 0.03). The lowest consistency was observed for AU7 (lid tightener; M = 0.57, SD = 0.22), AU17 (chin raiser; M = 0.72, SD = 0.18), and AU6 (cheek raiser; M = 0.73, SD = 0.08).

Cross-avatar consistency differed significantly across animations (χ 2 (17) = 94.409, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.93). Post-hoc comparisons showed that animations with relatively low cross-avatar consistency (AU6, AU7, AU17, AU23) differed significantly from those with very high consistency (AU1, AU2, AU10, AU12, browsAU10; all ps < 0.05).

Thus, although landmark displacement varied in consistency across facial movements, it provided highly consistent motion estimates across avatars for most animations.

Spatial Correspondence with Expected Motion

To evaluate whether landmark displacement was spatially concentrated in facial regions expected to move for a given AU, we computed the ratio of mean displacement in AU-relevant landmarks to mean displacement in all remaining landmarks (Figure 4D). Across animations, AU-relevant landmarks showed nearly twice as much displacement as the remaining landmarks (M = 1.94, SD = .70), with no significant differences across avatars (χ 2 (3) = 5.133, p = 0.162, Kendall's W = 0.095).

All animations yielded ratios above 1, indicating greater displacement in AU-relevant than in other facial landmarks. However, the magnitude of this spatial correspondence varied significantly across animations (χ 2 (17) = 58.474, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.86). The lowest ratios were observed for browsAll (M = 1.04, SD = 0.09), AU7 (lid tightener; M = 1.30, SD = 0.47), and AU6 (cheek raiser; M = 1.48, SD = 0.17). In contrast, the highest ratios occurred for AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 3.72, SD = 0.31), AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 2.92, SD = 0.14), AU4 (brow lowerer; M = 2.72, SD = 0.11), and AU12 (lip corner puller; M = 2.51, SD = 0.3).

Together, these results show that landmark displacement provided highly consistent estimates of facial motion across avatars and that displacement was systematically concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AUs. Although both cross-avatar consistency and spatial correspondence still varied across facial movements, the findings demonstrate the potential of landmark displacement for characterizing facial motion independently of AU predictions. Rigid head motion was removed using an inverse affine transformation, after which Euclidean displacement was computed relative to the initial neutral frame, yielding a 51 x 60 displacement matrix for each animation. (B) Mean pairwise correlations between avatars, averaged across animations, showing high consistency of landmark displacement patterns across avatars. (C) Mean cross-avatar correlations shown separately for each animation. Cross-avatar consistency was high for most facial movements, although it varied across animations. Discussion

In this study, we used controlled photorealistic facial animations with precisely specified motion to systematically evaluate methods for quantifying facial motion. By applying identical facial rigging parameters across MetaHuman avatars, we could assess how reliably different methods captured known facial motion while varying the face on which that motion was expressed. Our goals were threefold: first, to characterize the performance and potential biases of two widely used open-source AU-detection systems, OF and AFAR; second, to evaluate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry; and third, to provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates both approaches within a unified and reproducible framework.

Across analyses, automated AU-detection systems performed above chance but varied substantially across facial movements and avatars, and neither system reliably recovered the temporal dynamics of the specified AU trajectories. In contrast, landmark displacement yielded highly consistent motion estimates across avatars, with displacement systematically concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AUs. Together, these findings demonstrate the value of controlled stimuli with known motion parameters for evaluating facial motion quantification methods and highlight landmark displacement as a complementary approach for directly characterizing the geometric structure of facial motion.

Systematic Biases Revealed by Controlled AU Activations

By generating animations containing either isolated AUs or precisely controlled AU combinations, we could characterize systematic patterns in automated AU detection while knowing which facial movements were actually specified in each frame. Across OF and AFAR, we identified several recurring limitations that help explain when and why automated AU estimates may deviate from the underlying facial motion.

Overprediction of Smile-Related AUs

Both systems showed an increased tendency to predict smile-related AUs (particularly AU12 and AU14). These AUs were detected relatively well when present, but were also frequently predicted when absent, as reflected in their combination of high true-positive and false-positive rates. This pattern is consistent with previous evaluations reporting systematic confusions among commonly co-occurring facial actions (Guo et al., 2018; Namba et al., 2021 Namba et al., , 2022;; Perusquia-Hernandez et al., 2021). In particular, Namba and colleagues (2021) found that both OF and AFAR overpredicted co-occurrence of AU14 with AU6, AU10, and AU12.

One possible explanation is that automated AU detectors partly learn the statistical cooccurrence structure of facial actions in their training data rather than relying exclusively on the local visual changes associated with individual AUs. Previous work has shown that features informative for one AU can extend beyond its anatomically expected facial region. For example, AU6 can be predicted from mouth-region information, likely reflecting its frequent co-occurrence with AU12 during smiling (Ertugrul et al., 2019b). Such learned dependencies may be beneficial for recognizing naturally occurring expressions, in which AUs frequently co-occur, but can lead to systematic false positives when individual facial actions are experimentally manipulated in isolation. Our controlled animations make this distinction particularly apparent. That is, because the underlying AU activations were precisely specified, predictions of non-activated AUs can be directly distinguished from genuine co-occurring facial motion.

Better Temporal Correspondence for Combined-AU Animations

For several AUs, including AU10, AU15, and AU23, both systems showed greater temporal correspondence with the ground-truth trajectories when these AUs occurred in combination with other facial movements than when they were presented in isolation. Although perhaps counterintuitive, this finding is consistent with the co-occurrence effect described above. Naturally occurring facial expressions typically comprise combinations of facial actions, and AU detectors trained on such data may therefore learn statistical dependencies between frequently co-occurring AUs. As a consequence, an AU presented in a familiar combination may be easier to detect than the same movement presented in isolation.

Interestingly, this bias is in line with perceptual phenomena where humans perceive illusory slowing of feature motion when another facial feature is moving (Cook et al., 2015). Our controlled animations provide a useful framework for investigating such dependencies because individual AUs and their combinations can be manipulated independently while keeping their activation trajectories precisely specified. More broadly, synthetic facial animations could also be used to systematically vary AU co-occurrence during model training, providing a means to test whether more balanced exposure to isolated and combined facial actions improves the ability of AU-detection systems to recover individual facial movements.

Differences in Predicted AU Performance Across Avatars

We observed systematic differences across avatars, with both TPR and FPR higher for the two male avatars relative to the two female avatars. Importantly, the simultaneous increase in true-and false-positive rates suggests a greater tendency to predict AU presence for these avatars rather than uniformly better detection performance. Although this pattern could indicate gender-related differences, our sample of four avatars is too small to substantiate this interpretation. Gender was also confounded with other factors (such as skin tone, facial structure, and textures) in our stimulus set.

Nevertheless, the finding that identical AU activation parameters produced different prediction patterns across avatars indicates that automated AU estimates depend not only on facial motion but also on the face on which that motion is expressed. Such dependencies could potentially reflect biases in the demographic and visual composition of the datasets used to train AU-detection systems (Ertugrul et al., 2020). Systematically varying individual facial characteristics while holding the underlying motion constant provides a promising approach for identifying the sources of these dependencies in future work.

Differences Across Facial Actions

Some AUs, particularly AU6 and AU7, and to a lesser extent AU23 and AU17, showed notably poorer performance. Interestingly, AU6 and AU7 were also among the movements showing the lowest cross-avatar consistency and spatial correspondence in the landmarkdisplacement analysis. One possible explanation is that these facial actions are expressed partly through local surface deformation, such as cheek raising, eyelid tightening, and changes in skin shape, which may not be fully captured by the displacement of a sparse set of facial landmarks.

Consistent with this possibility, previous work has highlighted the importance of appearance information for detecting facial actions whose expressions involve local changes in facial shape and texture (Namba et al., 2021; Zhi et al., 2020).

Importantly, however, the limitations observed for AU detection cannot be attributed solely to landmark-based representations, as OF and AFAR incorporate additional visual information when predicting AUs. The convergence across AU detection and landmark displacement instead suggests that some facial movements may be intrinsically more difficult to quantify from standard video-based representations than others, even under highly controlled viewing conditions. Future work could test whether richer representations of facial surface deformation, including 3D mesh motion, depth or surface-normal information, improve the quantification of these movements.

Contribution of Landmark Displacement Analysis

The landmark-displacement analysis provided a complementary picture of facial motion to that obtained from automated AU detection. Despite identical motion parameters across avatars, AU predictions varied systematically across faces and facial movements. In contrast, landmark displacement patterns were highly consistent across avatars for most animations, and displacement was concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AU.

An important distinction between the two approaches lies in what they aim to estimate.

AU detection maps visual information onto predefined semantic action categories, requiring

an inference from the observed facial appearance and motion to an AU label. This mapping can be influenced by statistical regularities in the training data, including AU co-occurrence, imbalanced AU frequencies, and variations in facial appearance. Landmark displacement instead operates directly on tracked facial geometry, quantifying changes in landmark position without requiring these changes to be assigned to an AU category. Our results show that this simpler representation can recover highly consistent patterns of geometric motion across different avatars when the underlying animation parameters are held constant.

This advantage comes with an important trade-off. Landmark displacement describes the magnitude and spatial distribution of facial motion but does not provide the anatomical and semantic interpretation provided by FACS-based AU labels. Moreover, because our implementation relies on automatically tracked landmarks, it remains dependent on the accuracy and potential biases of the underlying landmark detector. Landmark displacement should therefore not be viewed as a replacement for AU detection, but as a complementary representation that is particularly useful when the primary question concerns the spatial and temporal structure of facial motion rather than its classification into predefined facial actions.

Implications for Facial Motion Quantification

Our findings highlight the complementary information provided by different representations of facial motion. Landmark displacement directly captures changes in facial geometry but may be less sensitive to facial actions expressed primarily through local surface deformation or appearance changes. AU-detection systems can incorporate such appearance information, but introduce an additional inference step that may be influenced by learned co-occurrence statistics and variation in facial appearance. Future approaches could therefore benefit from integrating multiple sources of information, including sparse or dense geometric motion, appearance, and 3D surface deformation, depending on the aspect of facial motion being quantified.

Controlled synthetic stimuli provide a useful framework for developing and evaluating such methods. Facial actions can be manipulated independently, combined systematically, and reproduced across different faces while their underlying motion parameters remain known.

Beyond benchmarking existing methods, such stimuli could therefore be used to systematically manipulate AU co-occurrence and facial appearance during model development, helping to determine which representations and training distributions support more robust quantification of facial motion.

To facilitate the application and evaluation of facial motion quantification methods, we developed FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified framework. By standardizing data processing and output formats across methods, FACET enables researchers to apply and compare different approaches within a reproducible workflow. Combined with controlled facial animations with known motion parameters, it also provides a foundation for systematically evaluating existing methods and developing improved approaches to facial motion quantification.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings. First, our stimulus set comprised a small number of photorealistic adult MetaHuman avatars.

Although these avatars were selected to resemble identities commonly represented in existing AU-detection datasets, they do not capture the full diversity of facial morphology, age, or skin properties present in real-world populations. Future work could systematically vary individual facial characteristics while holding motion constant to determine which aspects of facial appearance influence different facial motion quantification methods.

Second, the animations used here were intentionally short and highly controlled, with smooth, scripted motion trajectories designed to isolate specific facial actions. While this level of control is essential for diagnostic model evaluation, it does not capture the temporal complexity of spontaneous facial behavior, including micro-expressions, asymmetric motion, speech-related dynamics, or context-dependent expressions. Extending this approach to longer, more variable, and more naturalistic motion sequences would help determine how the observed patterns generalize beyond controlled facial animations.

Third, landmark displacement lacks the semantic interpretability inherent to FACSbased representations (Ekman et al., 2002) and depends on the accuracy of the underlying landmark tracker. Future work should assess the robustness of this approach across different landmark detectors or explore denser representations, such as 3D facial meshes, to better capture local surface deformation.

Conclusion

Reliable quantification of facial motion is essential for studying how we perceive and understand dynamic faces. By combining controlled photorealistic animations with AU-and landmark-based analyses, we show both the limitations of current AU-detection systems and the potential of landmark displacement as a complementary measure of facial motion. With FACET, we provide an open and reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion in experimental data and systematically evaluating the methods used to capture it.

AU independently of a specific decision threshold, we calculated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) from the continuous AU predictions. An AUC of 0.5 indicates chance-level discrimination. To characterize detection sensitivity and false alarms at the selected threshold, we additionally computed the true-positive rate (TPR) and falsepositive rate (FPR). TPR corresponds to the proportion of AU-present frames correctly classified as containing the AU, whereas FPR corresponds to the proportion of AU-absent frames incorrectly classified as containing the AU.Classification metrics and inferential statistics were calculated in Python (v3.10.6) using custom scripts and functions from the scikit-learn.metrics module(Pedregosa et al., 2011) and the pingouin package(Vallat, 2018), respectively. Depending on whether the data met the assumptions of parametric tests, comparisons between detection systems were conducted using paired-samples t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, whereas comparisons across avatars and animations were conducted using repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman test. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Lastly, to test whether the ROC AUC exceeded chance level (0.5), we ran one-sample t-tests. Effect sizes were reported alongside inferential statistics: Cohen's d for t-tests, rank-biserial correlation (rRBC) for Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and Kendall's W for Friedman tests.
